newsitem.title: UZBEKISTAN: Uzbekistan urged to diversify raw materials output.
newsitem.headline: Uzbekistan urged to diversify raw materials output.

text.p: The key to Uzbekistan's long term economic growth is a rich and varied commodity base, Robert Pace, executive director of the American-Uzbekistan Chamber of Commerce, said on Thursday.

While some Central Asian countries were heavily dependent on oil and gas, Uzbekistan also boasted some of the world's richest deposits of gold, as well as major reserves of copper, zinc, silver, molybdenum, uranium and coal, he said.
The former Soviet republic is also one of the world's largest cotton producers and exporters.
"One of the great attractions of the Uzbek economy in the future is its great variety," he told an oil and gas conference.

Pace said the balance between different commodities would probably shift, particularly in a move away from cotton production, which had been disastrous for the environment during the last few decades.
"Uzbekistan was the former Soviet Union's chief cotton producer, but it then suffered from an excessive dependence on cotton," Pace said.
"The country is now moving steadily away from cotton, and is seeking to expand grain and vegetable production and develop the food processing industry."
Uzbekistan was the world's second biggest cotton exporter in 1995, delivering 1.05 million tonnes of cotton fibre, according to International Cotton Advisory Committee figures.
Output fell in 1996 due to harsh weather conditions, but cotton remains a major export earner.
However, irrigation is costly, financially and environmentally, and Uzbekistan may do better to switch away from cotton to grain, Pace said.
It expects to import 1.0 to 1.2 million tonnes of grain, mostly from former Soviet neighbours, in 1997 after a disastrous 1996 harvest of 2.7 million tonnes.
"That is why the government is taking a more balanced approach, reducing some cotton production and increasing grains," Pace said.

Uzbekistan aims to produce 4.0 million tonnes of grain this year, almost meeting its 4.0-4.5 million tonnes annual demand. Pace said he saw a long-term target of grain self-sufficiency as "very realistic".

Uzbekistan also has ambitious expansion plans for the hydrocarbon sector, aiming to boost oil and gas condensate production this year to 8.0 million tonnes (160,000 barrels per day) and to 10.0 million (200,000 bpd) by 2000.
"That seems a realistic target," said Neil Smith, vice-president of Unocal of the U.S.
The country produced around 50 billion cubic metres of natural gas last year.

It aims to boost gold output by 100 percent within five years from current levels of 60 tonnes a year. Industry sources said the target seemed unrealistically high, but expected to see a healthy pick-up in output in the medium term.
Uranium output was 1,700 tonnes in 1996, and officials see production nearly doubling by 1999.
